sections.heading: Cost & delays
body:
Original estimate (2016): **£18bn**
Latest estimate (Feb 2026): {red:£35bn} in 2015 prices, nearly double.
Original completion: 2025. Current forecast: Unit 1 in {amber:2030}.

sections.heading: What the 35-year strike price means
body: HPC's CfD was agreed in 2013 at **£92.50/MWh in 2012 prices**. Indexed for inflation, that's roughly {amber:£130/MWh} today (it had already been indexed to £128.09 by 2024).

At current wholesale prices of ~£80–120/MWh, HPC would be {red:more expensive than the market}. Once it is generating, the LCCC would pay EDF the shortfall, roughly {red:£250m–£1.3bn per year} at those prices (our estimate).

Over 35 years and ~25.7 TWh/year output, the total support bill could be around {red:£9–45bn} if prices stayed in that range (our estimate), though payments reverse when prices spike (at 2022 prices, EDF would have been paying back).

The argument for HPC is long-term price stability: consumers are protected from future gas spikes. The argument against is that the strike price was set when renewables were far more expensive; recent offshore wind CfDs (2022–24 rounds) are roughly {green:£54–85/MWh} in today's money, well below HPC.
sections.footnote: EDF says HPC will supply around 7% of Britain's electricity. Despite the cost, it provides firm, weather-independent generation that wind and solar cannot, and that has real system value.

sections.heading: Status & cost
body: Final Investment Decision signed in July 2025 at around {amber:£38bn} (2024 prices). The government is the largest shareholder (44.9%), alongside La Caisse (20%), Centrica (15%), EDF (12.5%) and Amber Infrastructure (7.6%).

sections.heading: RAB model: you pay during construction
body: Unlike HPC's CfD, Sizewell C is funded under a **Regulated Asset Base (RAB)** model. Consumers pay a levy on their bills {amber:during construction}, years before any electricity is generated. It's estimated at around £1 a month for an average household. This reduces EDF/government financing costs but shifts risk to bill-payers.

Because SZC is a near-identical copy of HPC (same EPR design), the hope is that lessons learned mean {green:faster, cheaper construction}, though this remains to be proven, as every EPR built globally has overrun significantly.

sections.heading: No strike price: RAB instead
body: Because it is funded through RAB, Sizewell C does not have a CfD strike price like HPC. Its allowed revenue is regulated by Ofgem, so what consumers ultimately pay depends on how construction costs turn out.
